summary: Pupils aged 12–13 learn to classify chemical reactions into four families — combustion (burning a fuel in oxygen, releasing heat/light), oxidation (a substance gains oxygen, including rusting), thermal decomposition (heat breaks one compound into simpler substances), and displacement (a more reactive element takes another's place) — by reasoning from observable evidence and word equations, while checking that atoms (and therefore total mass) are conserved. The core skill is sorting NEW reactions into the right family from evidence, recognising that categories can overlap (burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation).
misconceptions: Assuming the four categories are mutually exclusive, when e.g. burning magnesium is both combustion and oxidation.
Confusing thermal decomposition (heat splits one substance apart) with reactions that combine substances, or thinking heating always causes decomposition.
Thinking oxidation only means rusting, missing that any gain of oxygen (including vigorous burning) is oxidation.
Believing combustion 'destroys' matter because the fuel seems to disappear, rather than forming gaseous products of equal mass.
Treating displacement as any two substances swapping, ignoring that the more reactive element must displace the less reactive one.

activities.title: Name that reaction: sort by evidence
steps: Take a shuffled set of reactions, some presented as word equations (e.g. copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide) and some as one-line observed scenes (e.g. a strip of magnesium flares white and leaves a powder; a piece of iron dipped in blue copper sulfate becomes coated with pink-brown metal).
Sort each reaction into one of four families: combustion, oxidation, thermal decomposition, displacement.
For each card, state the evidence that justifies your choice: heat and light, a gained oxide, one substance splitting apart on heating, or one element swapping for another.
Flag any reaction that seems to belong in two families and explain why (e.g. magnesium burning).
activities.insight: Each reaction family has a tell-tale observable signature, and you classify by reasoning from that evidence rather than by memorising definitions in isolation; some reactions legitimately belong to more than one family.

activities.title: Complete the word equation and check conservation
steps: Complete word equations with missing reactants or products, e.g. methane + oxygen -> carbon dioxide + water, and copper carbonate -> copper oxide + carbon dioxide.

After writing each equation, check that every element present before the reaction also appears after it. A word equation shows which elements are present, not how many atoms of each, so this check is consistent with atoms being neither created nor destroyed but does not prove it on its own.

Draw or compare before/after mass bars and explain that the TOTAL mass stays the same because atoms are only rearranged; then note that the solid you can actually weigh may appear to gain mass (magnesium takes in oxygen from the air) or lose mass (wood releases gases) depending on whether gas is absorbed or given off.
Match each reaction to its tell-tale sign: heat+light, gains oxygen, one substance splits into two or more simpler substances on heating, an element swapped out.
activities.insight: Reactions rearrange atoms rather than create or destroy matter, so total mass is conserved even when the weighable solid appears to change; word equations and the atom check make this explicit for every reaction type.

activities.title: Reaction bench: observe the signatures before sorting
steps: Visit four stations that each trigger one reaction type: light a fuel (combustion, heat and light), heat a metal in oxygen (oxidation, an oxide forms), heat a carbonate so the released gas turns limewater cloudy (thermal decomposition, CO2 detected), and dip a metal into a solution of a salt of a less reactive metal, e.g. iron into copper sulfate (displacement, a metal deposits with a colour change).
Watch each reaction auto-produce its word equation and note the observable signature.
Switch to a 'name that reaction' mode where the label is hidden and classify each reaction from its evidence alone.
activities.insight: Seeing each reaction type and its signature (flame, oxide layer, gas released on heating, deposited metal) is intended to build perceptual hooks that later classification can draw on.

activities.title: Predict–Observe–Explain: weighing burning magnesium
steps: Before burning, weigh a coil of magnesium ribbon and predict whether the mass of the white powder afterwards will be more, less, or the same — and state WHY.

Heat the ribbon in a crucible with a lid, lifting the lid slightly now and then to let air in while keeping the white smoke in. Then weigh the crucible, lid and product and compare with the crucible, lid and ribbon before heating.
Compare your prediction with the result and explain what combustion/oxidation actually did to the magnesium.
Reconcile this with wood burning, which leaves only light ash: where did the wood's mass go?
activities.insight: Combustion of magnesium is oxidation: the metal combines with oxygen from the air, so the solid product gains mass. Burning does not destroy matter; where mass seems to be lost (wood, candle) it has escaped as gases, so total matter is conserved.

activities.title: Complete vs incomplete combustion
steps: Compare complete combustion of a hydrocarbon fuel such as methane or candle wax (products carbon dioxide and water) with its incomplete combustion (products including carbon monoxide and soot).
Identify, from described evidence such as soot deposits or a smoky yellow flame, whether combustion was complete or incomplete.
Explain why limited oxygen leads to incomplete combustion and the formation of soot and carbon monoxide.
activities.insight: Combustion is not a single outcome: the amount of available oxygen changes the products, distinguishing clean complete combustion from sooty incomplete combustion.

checkQuestion: I burn a coil of magnesium ribbon in air and it leaves a white powder (magnesium oxide). A student says 'burning always destroys stuff, so the white powder must weigh LESS than the ribbon.' Would the powder weigh less, more, or the same — and the important part, explain what combustion/oxidation actually does to the magnesium.
checkAnswer: The white powder weighs MORE than the ribbon. Combustion here is oxidation: the magnesium GAINS oxygen from the air, combining with it to form magnesium oxide — so the added oxygen adds mass. Burning doesn't destroy matter; it combines the fuel with oxygen. Full marks explain the mass increase by oxygen being added, not by anything being 'used up'.
